Do not use colons.

text:
In late August 1854, a terrible sickness fell upon Soho, a crowded, working-class district of London. The disease was cholera, which causes violent vomiting and diarrhea and can kill a healthy adult within a day or two by draining the body of water. Within a few days of its arrival, hundreds of people living near Broad Street were dead. Many of the survivors fled the neighborhood, and shops stood shuttered. One local clergyman later estimated that three-quarters of the residents had left.

In 1854 nobody knew what caused cholera. Doctors had no microscopes powerful enough to settle the matter, and germs were not yet an accepted explanation for disease. The prevailing belief was the miasma theory, which held that illness spread through foul air rising from rotting waste, sewers, and marshes. It was a reasonable guess in a city that stank. London was filthy, and cesspools overflowed beneath many homes. But it was wrong.

John Snow, a physician living a short walk from Broad Street, had never believed it. Snow was a quiet, careful man who did not drink alcohol and who had made his name pioneering the use of anesthesia. He had even given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. Years earlier, during a cholera epidemic in 1848 and 1849, he had developed a different idea. He suspected that cholera was swallowed, not breathed. Something in contaminated water, he argued, carried the illness from one person's gut to another's. He had published this theory in 1849, and the medical establishment had largely ignored it.

The Broad Street outbreak gave him a chance to test his idea on a small, well-defined patch of streets. Snow went door to door. He sought out the families of the dead, and he asked a simple question: where did you get your water? In those days, most households did not have running water. People collected it from public pumps, and the water came from wells dug into the ground or from companies that piped river water into the city. Snow wanted to know which pump each victim had used.

He also obtained the official records of deaths from the local registrar and began plotting them on a map of the neighborhood. Each death was marked with a small black bar at the address where it occurred. When he looked at the map, a pattern emerged. The bars clustered thickly around a single water pump on Broad Street, near the corner with Cambridge Street. The closer a house was to that pump, the more deaths it tended to have.

Snow was careful, though, because a cluster could be a coincidence. He checked the exceptions, and the exceptions proved revealing. A workhouse nearby housed hundreds of poor residents, yet very few of them died. Snow discovered that the workhouse had its own well on the premises, so its inmates never needed the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the same street also lost no workers to cholera. The brewery staff were given a daily allowance of beer, and they also had their own well, so they had little reason to drink from the pump.

Other cases pointed the same way. A widow living far away in Hampstead, in northern London, died of cholera after a stay in the neighborhood had ended. Her family explained that she liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had a bottle of it brought to her each day. Her niece, who drank from the same bottle, died as well. Nobody else in their area fell ill.

By about the first of September, Snow felt confident enough to act. He presented his findings to the local board of guardians, the officials responsible for the parish. On September 8, they agreed to have the handle removed from the Broad Street pump, so that no one could draw water from it. The outbreak was already declining by then, perhaps because so many residents had fled or died, and skeptics later argued that removing the handle made little difference. Still, the gesture became legendary.

The immediate response to Snow's work was cool. A committee investigating the outbreak found his theory interesting but unproven. It did not accept that the water was to blame. Yet a local curate named Henry Whitehead, who had begun the investigation as a skeptic, ended up becoming Snow's ally. Whitehead dug deeper and found what Snow had missed, the likely start of the outbreak. A baby girl living at 40 Broad Street had fallen ill with diarrhea just before the epidemic began. Her mother had washed the baby's soiled cloths and thrown the dirty water into a cesspool only a few feet from the well. The cesspool was leaking into it.

John Snow died in 1858, still not fully recognized for what he had accomplished. Only in the following decades, as germ theory took hold and scientists identified the bacterium behind cholera, did his work earn its due. Today he is remembered as a founder of modern epidemiology, the study of how disease spreads through populations. His method of mapping cases, questioning people, and testing a hypothesis against the exceptions remains the foundation of public health detective work.
